The walk skips `.git`, `node_modules`, `bin` and `dist`, and doesn't descend
into a project once matched (projects don't nest). Projects with an unreadable
record are reported as warnings on stderr without hiding the rest.

## Systems (`intropy sys`)

### Assemble a system host

Run from the workspace root that holds your scaffolded integrations:

```sh
intropy sys create -n OrderFlow -o system-host   # -o is --out-dir here
```

The command reads before it writes: it scans the workspace for the
`.intropy/scaffold.json` records the integration scaffolds left behind,
validates them into a system model, and passes the assembled values to
the `system-host` template (a .NET Aspire AppHost), which renders the
whole declaration — `Topics.cs` defines each topic once as a
`TopicRef<T>`, `Ports.cs` defines each edge block's port to the outside
world (its deployed transport shape — connection values are deployment
configuration), and the `ISystemDefinition` class wires every extractor
and loader to its topic plus its port (`.From(...)` on extractors,
`.To(...)` on loaders) and the platform services (`.Uses(...)`). The workspace's shared contracts project (template role
`shared-library`, typically `Contracts/`) is referenced from the host's
project file, never declared as a component. A contracts project is only
needed when the system has topics: a host of transactional integrations
alone renders with no `Topics.cs` and no contracts reference, and a
topic-bearing system whose workspace lacks one gets it scaffolded by the
host template itself.

The generated development definition (`<Project>Development.cs`) owns the
local-run picture: it mocks the platform services from the skeleton's
OpenAPI documents and resolves each port to a drop folder under the
host's `test/` directory, so the assembled system runs end-to-end with
zero external configuration — drop a file into `test/<name>-source/`,
collect the result from `test/<name>-destination/`.

`-n` accepts PascalCase or kebab-case — `OrderFlow` kebab-cases to
`order-flow`, the system's name. Unlike `int create` there are no `--set`
or values flags: the CLI assembles every value from the scaffold records,
and the template never prompts.

This CLI renders against the current `system-host` release; pin an older
one with `--template-version`.

```sh
# default output directory: the kebab-cased name (./order-flow)
intropy sys create -n OrderFlow

# pin the system-host template release
intropy sys create -n OrderFlow -o system-host --template-version v1.5.0

content.text: Let me check how the dashboard's JSON flow shapes get rendered, so the overlay idea can be judged concretely.

I have a full picture now. Short answer: **moderately hard — a clean, well-sized feature.** The hard part is correlating Aspire spans to your topology nodes; the dashboard plumbing around it is easy. Here's the honest breakdown, with no changes made.

## What already lines up in your favor

- **The instrumentation story is free.** The `system-host` template is a .NET Aspire AppHost, and every system assembled by `sys create` runs through it. Aspire's OTLP telemetry is on by default (`DOTNET_DASHBOARD_OTLP_ENDPOINT_URL`), and Aspire's *own dashboard* (running on the AppHost, typically `localhost:18888` in dev, `localhost:17199` in containers) exposes a full **OTLP/HTTP JSON query API**: `/api/traces`, `/api/traces/{id}`, `/api/logs`, `/api/resources`. No extra sidecar, no schema to invent — the trace backend already exists the moment the AppHost runs.
- **Correlation keys are already on the wire.** Your topology's components are .NET services launched by the AppHost, so every span carries `service.name` = the Dapr/AppHost resource name — which is (or is one config line away from being) the same name as `TopologyComponent.name`. The dashboard joins graphs on that name everywhere already (`component:<name>`, `topic:<pubsub>/<topic>`), so a span's `service.name` is a direct join key.
- **The "show nothing when not running" requirement is trivial.** `GET http://localhost:18888/api/resources` either connects or it doesn't. Connection refused = AppHost down = render nothing. There's no ambiguity, no half-state, no cluster to query. (Caveat: Aspire 13 has `/login` auth on that dashboard API, so the fetch may need a token from the AppHost's stdout — that's the one real config knob.)
- **The server pattern already fits.** The dashboard deliberately derives nothing on the frontend; it proxies Go-side commands (topology, deploy status) and passes results through verbatim. Adding an `aspireProvider` alongside `topologyProvider`/`deployProvider` is the *same* shape — a new `internal/dashboard/traces.go` that calls the Aspire dashboard and re-emits spans — not a new architectural direction.

## The shape it would take

- **Server**: one new provider, one endpoint — `GET /api/traces?system=<path>` — that fans out to the local Aspire dashboard's OTLP query API, filters spans whose `service.name` matches a component in the current topology, and returns a per-node summary (span count, error rate, p50/p99, last-seen). Failure/absence of Aspire returns `204`/empty, and the frontend renders nothing.
- **Frontend**: the existing `IntNodeData` gets an optional `runtime?: { spans, errors, latency }` field; `IntegrationNode` renders a small badge/sparkline only when `runtime` is present. Topic and port nodes can do the same from span attributes (`messaging.destination` for topics). Edges could animate on live span flow, but that's polish, not core.
- **Polling**: a `setInterval` re-fetch (every ~5s) drives the "live" feel; when Aspire is down every poll just returns empty and the canvas stays clean. No manual state machine.

## Where the effort actually lives

- **Name matching is the only genuinely fiddly bit.** Aspire service names come from the AppHost's `.AddProject<...>("name")` calls; your topology names come from the `ISystemDefinition` wiring. They *should* be the same strings if the host template names resources after components — and if they aren't today, the fix is a one-line rename in the host template, not new plumbing. Worth verifying against a real generated AppHost before committing to the join.
- **Topic-level spans need Dapr/pubsub instrumentation attributes** (`messaging.system: dapr`, `messaging.destination: <topic>`), which .NET's `System.Net.Http`/Dapr instrumentation emits by default — but you'd confirm the attribute keys on a real trace before hard-coding them.
- **Auth + discovery**: which port the Aspire dashboard is on, and the login token in Aspire 13. Both are discoverable from the AppHost process, but it's the kind of thing that eats an hour of "why is this a 401" if you assume the defaults.

## Verdict

**Not hard as features go — call it a focused few days, not a rewrite.** The dashboard is a static-topology renderer today, and this makes it live, but the seams are already there: a third provider, a new endpoint, an optional field on node data. The riskiest unknown is service-name correlation; if that's already consistent, the rest is mostly mechanical. The cleanest first increment is component-node overlays only (count + error badge), leaving topic/edge animation as a follow-up.

Want me to verify the service-name correlation by inspecting an actual generated `system-host` (the `AddProject` resource names vs. `ISystemDefinition` component names)? That's the single fact that turns this from "moderately hard" into "straightforward."

Without making any changes can you suggest how we might use the telemetry data on the integration flow? The idea is perhaps not to show a lot of details but show a number of messages on the arrows between boxes and perhaps indicate with red (everything on this component have failed), yellow (some have failed), and green (everything has passed)

Good instinct — the flow view already reads as a diagram, so status should live *on* the diagram, not in a side panel. Here's how I'd map the Aspire data onto exactly what you described, plus the two or three decisions that determine whether it feels trustworthy or noisy. Still no changes made.

## The visual language

**Component cards get a traffic light, nothing more.** One small dot in the card header (next to the existing kind tag), four states:

- **no dot** — no spans seen for this service. This is your "not running → show nothing" rule, and it's the most important state: it must be visually *absent*, not grey. Grey reads as "unknown/idle" and users will mistake it for a status; absence reads as "not instrumented right now."
- **green** — spans seen in the window, zero with error status.
- **yellow** — some errored, some succeeded.
- **red** — everything in the window errored.

Hover tooltip carries the one line of detail: `42 spans, 3 errors, last 5 min`. No numbers on the card itself — the card stays a topology card.

**Edges get a count pill, nothing more.** React Flow edges already support a `label`, and your edges are built with stable IDs (`e:pub:<comp>:<pubsub>/<topic>`), so a label is a pure data merge: `label: '127'`, styled as a small pill on the line. The count is **spans in the last N minutes**, not a lifetime total — a lifetime counter becomes meaningless wallpaper after a day, while a windowed count reads as throughput ("is anything flowing right now"), which is the question someone staring at this view is actually asking. Zero flow in the window = no pill, same show-nothing rule as the dots.

That's the whole overlay: dots on cards, pills on lines. It composes with everything already there (ghosts, slots, selection) because it touches only `IntNodeData` and the edge objects — no layout, no new node types.

## Mapping the Aspire data to it

The server does the shaping; the frontend stays dumb, consistent with the package's "derive nothing on the client" rule:

- **Per component**: filter spans by `service.name` (the correlation we discussed — verify it matches `TopologyComponent.name`), bucket by `status.code` over the window → `{ spans, errors }` per component name.
- **Per topic edge**: Dapr/pubsub spans carry messaging attributes (`messaging.destination` = topic, span kind producer/consumer). Count producer spans on the publish edge, consumer spans on the subscribe edge — or just total per topic if you don't care about direction, simpler and the count lands on the same topic node either way.
- **Per port edge**: spans touching the binding. This one is the fuzziest — port ↔ span correlation depends on what the binding instrumentation emits — so I'd ship it last, or not at all in v1. A port edge with no pill is fine; it already reads as "external."

One endpoint — `GET /api/traces?system=<path>` — returns `{ nodes: { name: {spans, errors} }, topics: { "pubsub/topic": count }, since: <window start> }`, or 204 when the Aspire dashboard is unreachable. `FlowView` polls it on a 5–10s interval alongside the existing topology state, merges into node data and edge labels in the `buildDeclaredGraph` memo, done. Unreachable Aspire = 204 every poll = clean static diagram, zero error UI.

## The decisions that make or break it

1. **The window defines "everything failed."** Red = 100% of spans errored *in the window*, and you need a minimum sample size — a component that ran once and threw once is not the same signal as one that's failed 200 times in a row. Something like: red needs ≥ 3 spans, all errored; below that, a single error is yellow. Otherwise the view cries wolf every time a scheduled extractor wakes up and hiccups once.
2. **Green means "spans seen, none errored" — not "healthy."** A silent-but-broken component shows no dot, same as a stopped one. That's honest given the data, but the tooltip wording should say "no spans in window," not "ok."
3. **Topic nodes could take the same dot.** A topic with recent publishes but zero successful consumer spans is a real, visible failure mode (messages piling up). Same traffic-light rule, derived from consumer spans. Cheap once the span bucketing exists; I'd include it.

## Sequencing

1. Component dots only — proves the Aspire connection, auth, and service-name correlation with the smallest possible UI surface.
2. Topic edge counts — the "messages on arrows" part, once attribute keys are confirmed against a real trace.
3. Topic node dots, port edges — if the correlation data cooperates.

Step 1 alone is maybe a day; steps 1–2 are the full feature you described. The only thing I'd nail down before writing any of it is the service-name correlation, since every join above hangs off it.
Similar to how we can see the logs for running the host could each component get a button to show the logs (from aspire) for that component?

content.text:
Good context — the host-logs pattern is now clear: the toolbar's **Logs** button toggles a `<pre>` tail of the host's combined stdout/stderr, served from the run supervisor's ring buffer. A per-component logs button is a natural extension, but it's a different data path. Here's how I'd do it.

## The key difference from the host log

The existing Logs panel is free because the dashboard *launched* the process — it owns the pipes, so the ring buffer is just there. Per-component logs can't come from that same stream for two reasons:

- The AppHost's own stdout mostly says "resource X started," not the components' application logs — Aspire components write to their own stdout, which the AppHost forwards to its **structured logging** pipeline, not verbatim to the host console.
- Mixing in a combined stream would require parsing which lines belong to which component — fragile, when Aspire already did the separation for us.

The right source is the Aspire dashboard's **OTLP logs API** — `GET /api/logs?resource=<name>` on the local dashboard (the same connection as the traces overlay). It returns structured log records per resource: timestamp, severity, message, attributes. Structured from the start, per-component by design, and it works even for a host started outside the dashboard (e.g. from a terminal) — the traces connection and the logs connection are the same one, so the button lights up exactly when the run/telemetry connection is live.

## The shape it would take

**Button placement**: the integration card is dense already, and per your "not a lot of details" principle I'd put the button on the card only when telemetry is live — a small log icon next to the traffic-light dot, same conditional-visibility rule: no Aspire connection, no button. Alternatively (and arguably cleaner): put it in the inspector. Today clicking a *component* selects it, but components don't open an inspector the way topics/ports do — a component inspector panel that shows the log tail would give you the button plus room for the output, reusing the existing `FlowDetail` aside pattern.

**Viewer**: reuse the existing host-logs UI pattern, not invent a new one — a `<pre>` tail, toggled open/closed. Where the host panel is a fixed tail of the last 200 lines, the component version gets two cheap upgrades the structured data makes almost free:

- **Severity filter** — a checkbox row (errors only / warnings+ / all). This is the single most useful thing the Aspire data gives you over a raw stream, and it's just a filter on a field the API already returns.
- **Follow mode** — poll every 2–3s while the panel is open, append new records. Mirrors how the host panel already refreshes on poll.

**Server**: one more endpoint next to the traces one — `GET /api/logs?system=<path>&component=<name>` — that proxies the Aspire dashboard's logs API filtered by resource name (the same service-name correlation as traces), tail N records, and returns them verbatim-ish: `[{time, severity, message}]`. The dashboard derives nothing; it reshapes. Aspire unreachable → 204/empty → no button, per the standing rule.

## Where the effort is

Genuinely small once the traces connection exists — that's the point of sequencing it after the telemetry overlay:

- The hard prerequisite is exactly the one the traces feature already solves: discovering and authenticating to the Aspire dashboard, and the service-name ↔ component-name correlation. If that join is proven, this feature is "call a different endpoint on the same connection."
- The logs API returns structured records, so no line parsing, no ring buffer, no process ownership questions. It's a read-only proxy.
- The UI is the one place with real choices (button-on-card vs inspector panel, severity filter, follow mode), but all of it reuses existing components: `FlowDetail` aside, the `flow-run-logs` pre styling, the poll loop pattern.

One caveat worth naming: the Aspire dashboard's log retention is in-memory and bounded (it keeps a rolling window per resource, thousands of entries, not forever). So the panel is a *live tail*, not a log archive — "what is this component saying right now," which is exactly the debugging question someone clicking a button on the flow diagram is asking. If they need history, that's the full Aspire dashboard's job, and a "open in Aspire" link next to the button is a one-line escape hatch.

So: same difficulty class as the trace counts, cheaper than the traffic lights (no bucketing, no thresholds) — the natural third increment after dots and edge pills. Want me to spec out the three increments together as a plan?
